content:
sqlite sucks.
It saddens me that every time I see some cool Roc web or app framework, the storage layer is sqlite. I instantly lose interest in any Roc project where I see SQL, especially in the form of sqlite. Migrations are terrible, it has a dynamic schema, and a huge C library that needs platform support.
And SQL query language is so different, compared to Roc. This is the worst thing. Most of the logic is about conversion between the two paradigms.

SurrealDB is quite good, but it's not supported in any Roc framework, and it's more like a Postgres alternative, not an sqlite alternative. It's much better for web projects than Postgres. I would never use Postgres for anything, if I can use SurrealDB instead. But for simple apps, where basic object persistence is required, a separate database process is overkill.

I think, a new, pure-Roc in-process object persistence framework could be written in about ~6000 lines of Roc code. (Maybe even in ~4000 lines.) It could work with any platform that provides basic file I/O, and it could provide a much more ergonomic query language, i.e. everything that's possible in Roc, because it's pure Roc. And the whole Roc typesystem, (including tag unions and other niceties) could be used for storing data.

Basic feature set that would be useful:

  • Migrations, with mandatory error handling. Roc's error handling is a huge utility for this.
  • Transactions with rollback. I think, Roc immutability can help a lot.
  • Nested data, not just top level fields per record. Two dimensional data is a limitation in SQL.
  • Link constraints (a.k.a. foreign-key constraints in SQL). Also in nested data, see SurrealDB for how it works.
  • Full ACID compliance.
  • Plain Roc query language, no special syntax.
  • Data manipulation should be pure, and syncing to storage is the only effectful thing.

I have some architecture ideas, and I'll write them here soon, but meanwhile if anyone is interested in this, dump ideas here.

Let's design the in-process database for the next generation of Roc apps together!

Sqlite is pretty awesome. Watch some of the creators talks on the technical aspects of testing. It's kind of legendary. Also you have been enforce a strict schema for a long time now.

Other directions I'm really interested in thinking about besides sequel light is something like Rich Hickey's datomic
Oh, I didn't meant to disregard the engineering achievements of the project. There's so much to learn from it. But SQL (any dialect) is a terrible language to work with.
I used EdgeDB, which was quite good, but still limited by how Postgres arranged data in 2 dimensions.
But EdgeQL was much better than SQL.
When the project got abandoned, I moved to SurrealDB, which allows tree-like data, and ADT.
But I'm not satisfied with it either. (Tooling is weak.)
It's nice until it has to be used in a different language. It requires so much plumbing.
(Just like SQL.)
Type-checking the queries should require multiple GiB of RAM, yet it does with SQL:
https://github.com/niclas-ahden/roc-pg-insane-in-the-membrane
Datomic is interesting, I have not heard of it until now.
Checked it out, but it's quite different from how I would imagine a Roc in-memory database.
I have fond memories of dBase haha. (It had its own procedural language.)
SpacetimeDB is a really fast in-memory db (with persistence) providing a redux-like functional API
A database that treats data in rows and columns instead of a tree-like structure is not an option.
In my experience, 2 dimensional layout often requires a few other tables, which increases complexity, and reduces readability.
My goal with this idea is not to replicate other databases in Roc, but to find the most ergonomic way to manage persisted data in Roc.

Why not just a typed EdgeQL style front end, in Roc, on a known acid compliant engine?

Also I don't know how you would get both strict typing and also avoid migrations. most migrationless systems just force the client to handle nulls all over and you get bad user experience with lots of bugs. (or you limit schema changes like protobuf does.

Also I don't know how you would get both strict typing and also avoid migrations.

I want typed migrations with mandatory error handling. For example, most ORMs allow you to write a migration that changes an optional text field to a required one. Then, if the production DB has one record where that field is null, the migration fails. But it should be possible to type this field modification as returning Try({}, [IncompatibleValue]), so it's obvious when writing the migrations that it can fail, and has to be explicitly handled. This is a very simple example, but as the schema gets more complex, there are many more ways to fail, and if it's not tracked in the type system, migrations can quickly become a bad experience.

Why not just a typed EdgeQL style front end, in Roc, on a known acid compliant engine?

If the whole data is in memory, queries can be very readable. So it's more like an object persistence library than a DB engine, as the “query optimizer” would be the Roc compiler itself, because the queries are pure Roc functions.
If the data is elsewhere, and Roc code only builds queries, it's just indirection.
How would you implement an type-safe EdgeQL-style front end in Roc? Comptime parse the queries?
if the "whole data is in memory" how do you get the "D" in acid that "D" part is a huge huge portion of what make writing a db hard.
Not only in memory. More like a full in-memory copy of the disk content, not only for caching, but also for a nicer query interface. Sorry, I'm not really good at describing this idea.
